candidates.title: Is the SEC's Schedule Actually Harder, or Does the Rating Just Believe It Is?
candidates.number: SOS computed two ways: opponent-adjusted from results only (SRS, no priors) vs SP+ (carries preseason reputation). The gap between them IS the bias.
candidates.why: His exact ask: an unbiased SOS 'that does not completely cater to the SEC'. The trap is that most SOS numbers are partly circular -- a rating that already believes the SEC is strong will report SEC schedules as strong. Carry is enormous: same circularity runs credit scores, school rankings, hiring.

candidates.title: Which Coaches Shrink Against Good Teams?
candidates.number: record vs AP top-10 and top-25 opponents, residualised on the coach's own roster talent -- 'choke artist' as a measurable quantity
candidates.why: His words: 'we need a rank the coaching. How does a coach fare against an AP top 10 team versus a top 25 team?' Turns the most common bar argument in the sport into an estimate with an interval.

candidates.title: A First Season Is a Baseline, Not a Verdict
candidates.number: does year-1 record predict years 3-5, controlling for inherited roster? test on every FBS coaching change 2015-2025
candidates.why: His claim: 'you can never fire a coach after their first season.' Immediately live via Matt Campbell at Penn State. Carry: the difference between a measurement and a judgement.

candidates.title: Where Each Position Is Actually Grown
candidates.number: blue-chip recruits per capita by state AND position -- is it true that offensive linemen are not produced in the South?
candidates.why: His claim, stated flatly: 'o-linemen aren't bred in the South.' Either it holds or it doesn't; either way it is a clean map nobody publishes.
candidates.outcome: Issue #147 147-talent-addresses -- claim half right: the South makes blue-chip OL at 2.4x the national rate but only 0.63 per DL vs 0.98 elsewhere. Real finding was concentration: Gini 0.838 across 8,018 high schools, top 50 = 16% of all blue-chips.

candidates.why: Both of you landed on it independently: 'this American Conference might be a little bit stronger than we ever anticipated.' Falls out of the same machinery as the SOS piece.

candidates.title: What a Career Costs, Per Year of It
candidates.number: total cost to produce one pro athlete vs one racehorse, against expected productive years of each
candidates.why: Your own aside: 'what is the total cost of a player, and what is the total cost of a horse?' Bred for speed, not survival -- and the same is measurably true of running backs.

candidates.title: The Stat That Cannot Tell You Anything
candidates.number: out-of-sample predictive value of the split/streak stats broadcasts actually put on screen -- expected to be indistinguishable from zero
candidates.why: HELD, and the gate is honest: needs a defined sample of real broadcast graphics before it can be settled. Unlocks the moment someone logs 100 of them off a weekend of games. His archetype: a graphic comparing Philip Rivers to a cornerback by number of children.

candidates.title: Do Some Franchises Actually Ruin Players?
candidates.number: within-player before/after: performance and workload change for players arriving at vs leaving a franchise, player fixed effects. Browns, Jets, Bengals named; 'overused' is separately testable as snap share against position norms.
candidates.why: His claim, and he staked it: 'Cleveland is where players go to die... the stats are going to prove me right about this.' The trap is selection -- bad clubs ACQUIRE declining players, so the naive comparison confirms the claim spuriously. Only a within-player design can separate the institution from the intake. Carry is the whole ballgame: same confound as hospital mortality rates, school value-added, and every manager-effect study ever run. And he may be wrong, which would make it better.
candidates.outcome: Issue #149 149-where-players-die -- claim REFUTED. Cleveland 9th of 32 for keeping careers alive (+6.4 pts adj), 4th among established starters; overuse 15th of 32. Arizona and Washington are the graveyards.

candidates.title: Why We Take the Log of the Odds
candidates.number: the October bracket is the worked example: home field is ONE constant, +0.14 in log-odds, and it produces a different probability bump for a .500 club than a .700 one. Show the same edge added in probability space breaking (>1) and in log-odds space behaving.
candidates.why: Reader asked directly: why the log, and what is an odds ratio for. The bracket makes it concrete rather than abstract -- and the 2026 AL field hands us the hook: the projected No.1 seed would be an UNDERDOG in its own division series, 49%, because seeding rewards winning a division and the odds reward being good. Carry is a 10: log-odds is the engine under logistic regression, medical risk, credit scoring and every 'controlling for' claim anyone has ever read.
candidates.outcome: Issue #150 150-why-log-odds -- home field as ONE constant (+0.14) buying +3.5 / +2.9 / +1.2 points at .500 / .700 / .900; odds ratio 2.98 [2.35,3.78] from our own week-1 data against a risk ratio of 1.57, an 89% overstatement.

candidates.title: Two Markets, Nobody Talking, One Number
candidates.number: Kalshi and Polymarket World Series books, pulled 2026-08-31: mean absolute disagreement 0.15 percentage points across 29 clubs, largest 0.7 (Diamondbacks). Books sum to 100.2% and 100.8%.
candidates.why: Two venues with different mechanisms, currencies and regulators price the same 30 outcomes within a sixth of a point of each other. And neither quotes odds or a spread -- both sell a binary contract, so the PRICE IS THE PROBABILITY, no de-vigging. The overround comparison is the clean teachable: a bookmaker's margin is visible the moment you add the board up. Pairs with #150 on log-odds. VERIFY the typical sportsbook futures hold against three sources before printing a number for it.

candidates.title: The Positions the Box Score Cannot See
candidates.source: Patrick sr, 2026-08-31, from watching USC's freshman edge
candidates.number: by position, how well do college box-score stats predict where a man is actually drafted? Use NFL draft slot as the external criterion, college counting stats as the predictor. Expect near-zero for offensive line and low for edge; high for quarterback and receiver. The R-squared BY POSITION is the story.
candidates.why: Came out of a real case: USC's Luke Wafle, national #6 recruit, put up 2 tackles and half a TFL in his opener. The stat line is not evidence against him -- it is evidence the tackle column cannot see an edge rusher's job. Crucially this is NOT a small-sample problem: a hundred more games of tackle counts still would not answer it, because the measure is wrong rather than noisy. That distinction -- INVALID versus NOISY -- is the deepest idea in the curriculum and almost nobody separates them. Carries straight to teacher evaluations, performance reviews, hospital metrics and citation counts.

candidates.title: Ohtani's Cold October: Noise, Injury, or Not Clutch?
candidates.number: Postseason 2026: 3-for-20, 0 HR, 7 K in 24 PA (.411 OPS) vs .889 regular season. A 6-game window that cold is 1 in 125 of his windows since 2021 -- but he plays ~150 windows a year, so about one per season is expected (2026 regular season already had two). Biceps-inflammation IL Sep 8-23 is a real candidate cause. Dodgers went 3-1 in the NLDS while he hit 2-for-13.
candidates.why: Rare per window, routine per season: the same arithmetic as the CFB upset lesson. Hot hand and cold hand are one argument. The honest twist: not every slump is noise -- Issue #63 (Raleigh) found the oblique. Tests the 'slumping Ohtani = Dodgers lose' belief directly.

candidates.title: Who Actually Rises to the Occasion?
candidates.number: Year-to-year correlation of each qualified hitter's late-and-close (or RISP) OPS minus overall OPS, MLB Stats API splits. If clutch were a trait, this year's clutch gap predicts next year's. Then: who are the few with a persistent positive gap, and is Ohtani one?
candidates.why: The editor believes some people are clutch. The data has mostly said no, with small effects at most. Test it honestly, and name the people if they exist -- 'show me' is the standard.

candidates.title: When Does a Season Start Telling the Truth?
candidates.number: CFB: weeks of games before results outweigh the preseason prior, by program. Do we update faster on Indiana (no reputation, Cignetti) than on Alabama/Georgia (reputation = players)? Measure how much preseason rank still predicts final rank vs how much week-N results do.
candidates.why: Observations are not independent and are contaminated by expectation. 'Show me' fans versus believers. Carries to any judgment of a newcomer versus an incumbent.

candidates.title: Same Coach, Four Programs: How Much Is the Job?
candidates.number: Lou Holtz across William & Mary, NC State, Jets, Arkansas, Minnesota, Notre Dame, South Carolina: win% vs each program's baseline before and after him. Separates coach effect from situation (talent access, administration). Needs verified records.
candidates.why: Coach-by-situation interaction. 'You are only as good as your boss.' Pairs with the inherited-roster piece (#200). Answerability unconfirmed until the program baselines are pulled.

candidates.title: Everything We Worried About That Turned Out to Be Nothing
candidates.number: End of each season (MLB after the World Series, CFB after the title game): every early-season storyline the paper ran, scored as real / noise / missed. Plus what we never wrote about that mattered.
candidates.why: The paper as a fan that learns. Year one is the first full cycle; this is the annual accountability piece per sport. Sal's Sorsby column holds for the CFB end-of-season slot.

candidates.title: Believe It or Know It? (series)
candidates.number: Series: each entry takes one stat fans trust (record in close games, QB wins, 'knows how to win') and asks which stat, why, and believe-or-know -- then tests it. Launched by 178-book-it-bills-notre-dame. Bayes is the spine: belief as a prior, evidence as the update, certainty as the one prior that cannot learn.
candidates.why: Understanding your own biases. Reader-fed: the launch piece asks readers to send the stat they trust.

candidates.title: How Long Does a New Idea Last?
candidates.number: Half-life of a scheme's edge: for each named innovation (CFB: Briles Baylor spread, Leach Air Raid, Kelly Oregon, Malzahn; NFL: 2008 Wildcat, Kelly Eagles, McVay Rams, 2019 Ravens; defenses for contrast), the innovator's offensive or defensive efficiency vs league average (CFBD / nflverse EPA per play) in each season after debut, and the years until that edge falls by half.
candidates.why: His claim: offensive gimmicks get caught fast in the NFL and slowly in college, while an attacking defense built on personnel and aggression lasts longer. Two testable halves (pro vs college decay rate; offense vs defense). The trap is small n -- a handful of named schemes, chosen because they were famous -- and regression to the mean, which shrinks any outlier season whether or not a defense 'caught up'. Carry: why every edge in business decays once it is copied. Editor, 2026-10-19: the adjustment to a hot new scheme should come faster in the NFL (all players capable; scheming is the lever) than in college (buy-in and teaching take longer).

candidates.title: Can Anyone Spot a Great Offensive Lineman?
candidates.number: By position: how well does a recruit's star rating predict being drafted (and drafted early)? CFBD recruiting + draft data. Is the star-to-draft link weaker for OL than for skill positions? Second step: does combine size, or college starts (longevity), predict NFL starts for OL better than for others?
candidates.why: His hypothesis: high school to college is mostly size; college to pro is size, technique and longevity. Follows Issue #147 (where linemen come from) with a different question (whether anyone can tell which ones are good). Answerable with data we already pull.

candidates.title: Why Go Pro in Anything but Life?
candidates.number: Earnings distribution of pro athletes (median vs mean, by sport and NFL position, via nflverse/OverTheCap contracts), career length by position, and the cost side: pay per career snap. Test his claim that linemen are paid least (likely false at tackle -- running backs are the usual cheap position; check).
candidates.why: There are few Tiger Woods and many who scrape by. The mean salary is a skewed-distribution lie; the median is the honest number. Carry is maximal: the same skew governs actors, musicians, startups. Must not lecture; the number does the work. Sibling of player-vs-racehorse (Aug 11): that one is the cost side; build them as one piece or a pair.

candidates.title: How Many Times Does a Player Actually Get to Perform?
candidates.number: Per game, per player: golf ~70 strokes in four hours; a hitter ~4 plate appearances; an NFL starter ~60 snaps; plus pitches seen, touches. Count real chances to perform per game and per season, by sport and position, from MLB Stats API, nflverse snap counts, PGA scoring. Ties to the hot hand: fewer chances means noisier streaks.
candidates.why: Baseball is a game of waiting; football is waiting while fully engaged ('head on a swivel'). Sample size per game is the hidden variable under every hot-hand, slump and clutch argument -- this is the denominator piece for the whole series. Could pair with why-go-pro as cost per performance moment.

candidates.title: Two Notre Dame Men Are Running the Midwest
candidates.number: Pat Murphy (ND head coach 1988-94, Brewers manager) and Craig Counsell (played for him at ND; Cubs manager) -- verified via MLB Stats API coach rosters 2026-10-17; ND years need three sources. Brewers 103-59 (MLB best, swept LAD); Cubs led MLB in runs (850). Statistical half: where do Midwest-born pitchers come from and do they last longer (fewer innings as teenagers, healthier shoulders)? Birth state from MLB Stats API, career length / IL stints by birth region.
candidates.why: The editor's joy is the hook, but the issue needs a number: the 'cold-weather arms are fresher' hypothesis is testable and nobody publishes it. Bio facts about Murphy/Counsell must be triple-sourced; the editor first remembered Murphy's name wrong.

candidates.title: What Is a Goalie Worth?
candidates.number: Igor Shesterkin out for the season (knee, announced Oct 10; NHL.com, ESPN, ABC). Goals saved above expected per season from NHL API shot data, converted to standings points; compare to the best skaters' value. Then: the Rangers' points pace with their replacement goalies. Plus/minus is the wrong stat -- explain why.
candidates.why: His claim: the goalie is the most important player on the ice, and hockey's loser point makes preventing goals worth more than scoring them. Both halves are testable. Prior evidence says elite goalies are worth more wins than any skater, though they are also the least consistent from year to year.

candidates.title: How Hard Was It? (series: a schedule is a belief)
candidates.number: scripts/schedule_belief.py. Launched by 179. Follow-ups: (1) weekly trajectory of each contender's ranked-opponent count through 2026, re-run each Sunday; (2) end-of-season pre/post for every CFP team, not just champions; (3) NFL vs CFB: how much of a final ranking is settled head-to-head vs by proxy (share of top-25 pairs connected by a direct game or one common opponent).
candidates.why: His frame: the NFL is a randomized trial (designed schedule, settle it on the field), college football an observational study -- wide bandwidth, low fidelity, so it runs on belief. Bayesian spine: the preseason poll is the prior, Saturdays are the update. Pairs with believe-it-or-know-it.

candidates.title: Do runs go up after a pitching change?
candidates.number: Runs in the rest of the inning after a change vs base-out expected runs, by inning 1-9 (Retrosheet 2021-25)
candidates.why: Editor's bet: runs rise after a change in innings 4-6, not in the 8th/9th. The trap is selection: pitchers get pulled while being hit. Lesson: compare to what the situation was already worth.

candidates.title: How fast can a coach turn a program around?
candidates.number: Year-over-year SP+/win% jumps, FBS 2005-26; Indiana 2024 and UCLA 2026 against a regression-to-the-mean baseline
candidates.why: Both coaches came from James Madison. Bad teams improve anyway, so the story is the gap above that baseline. Ties to murphy-counsell-midwest (coaching trees).

candidates.title: How many points does it take to win in college?
candidates.number: Points thresholds for 50/75/90% wins, CFB vs NFL; season-level offense/defense trade-off; P(win | allow <=14); yards per play vs points
candidates.why: Sequel to the NFL win-probability page, read on the points axis instead of the probability axis. Editor's bet: defense can carry you in the NFL but not in college.
